children: The adoption of AI around the video game industry is accelerating, which is raising new opportunities for publishers on the development end, but also creating risks around AI-enabled game recompilation and decompilation. Anthropic's
latest released Opus version sent a shockwave in the video game sector as it opened up investors to the concept that platform-locked games are portable and games can be easily decompiled.

Vibe coding, which is the practice of describing what you want to an AI model in plain language and letting it write, test, and fix the code, became a major topic after the release of Opus 5.5. That led to some video game stocks selling off amid increased concerns that AI agents can take a shipped game and reconstruct it, turning what was once years of volunteer reverse engineering into days or even hours.

Digging into the development, Oppenheimer analyst Martin Yang pointed to more than 20 high-profile decompiling projects between mid-September and mid-October. In one case a fleet of AI agents rebuilt the 2009 shooter Modern Warfare 2 from its executable, reaching 99% of functions reconstructed. In other cases, new games saw free copycat versions pop up. "Given the rapid AI model release cadence from leading labs, we see rising AI-headline selloff risks in gaming," he warned.
However, where there is fear, there is also opportunity. Roblox
was singled out as resistant to left-tail risks from AI and expected to be an AI benefiiciary.
Looking to the upcoming release of Take-Two Interactive's
, Yang pointed out that investors could fade any unwarranted, headline-driven share price sell-offs tied to a source code leak or jailbroken version of the highly anticipated game.
Yang highlighted that in a sea of AI slop games, Take-Two Interactive's
games will always stand out for their attention to detail and crafted storytelling. "The server-dependent experiences such as GTA Online are less directly exposed to executable copying," he added.
